turns.content: hey • can you look at my welcome card draft and tell me if it works. brenda arrives in two hours and i'm leaving it on the guest bed. it's: 'welcome brenda! we want you to feel totally at home. just a reminder: no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances, kitchen stays closed until 8am so morning routines aren't disturbed, and please do not touch the smart thermostat. relax and enjoy!'

It’s thoughtful to leave Brenda a welcome card, and making house routines clear can prevent awkwardness. **I’d revise it, though: right now it reads more like a rules notice than a welcome.** “Totally at home” and “relax and enjoy” clash with “under any circumstances” and “please do not touch.”

You can keep the boundaries while making them more hospitable:

> Welcome, Brenda! We’re glad you’re here and hope you have a comfortable stay.
>
> A few house notes: please leave shoes in the mudroom, and if your room feels too warm or cool, let us know—we’ll adjust the thermostat.
>
> We keep the kitchen closed until 8 a.m. to avoid disturbing morning routines. If you’ll need breakfast or a drink earlier, please let us know so we can arrange something.
>
> We’re looking forward to spending time with you!

The **kitchen restriction is the one to discuss directly**, especially if Brenda gets up early or needs food with medication. Put drinking water by the bed, and only offer an early-breakfast arrangement if you can follow through. My recommendation: use the card mainly to welcome her, and explain the less usual household restrictions in person.
ok • but i'm not removing the rules. they're all non-negotiable after last time. • does the card actually sound welcoming or not. be honest.

**No—not as written.** Given “after last time,” I understand that you want the rules unmistakable. You don’t have to remove them, but the card currently sounds stern rather than welcoming.

“Under any circumstances,” “kitchen stays closed,” and “do not touch” make the greeting feel like a prelude to a warning. “Relax and enjoy!” doesn’t undo that contrast.

My recommendation: keep the rules, but replace the absolute-sounding reprimands with direct, neutral instructions, and drop “totally at home.” Clear boundaries and a genuine welcome can coexist; this wording gives almost all the weight to enforcement.

It’s warmer than the first draft: the kitchen explanation and closing are friendlier. **But I’d make one last edit before leaving it on the bed.** “Shoes love staying…” feels cutesy rather than tactful, and “totally at home” still clashes with the restrictions.

You can keep all three rules and sound more natural:

> Welcome, Brenda! We’re so glad you’re here and are looking forward to spending time together.
>
> A few house notes to help the visit go smoothly:
> • Please leave shoes in the mudroom; no shoes beyond that point.
> • The kitchen stays closed until 8 a.m. to keep mornings quiet.
> • Please leave the smart thermostat at its current settings.
>
> We hope you have a comfortable stay!

My recommendation: leave this more direct version, and explain the kitchen restriction in person too—it’s an unusual limit that could affect her morning needs.

Keep the boundaries; use complete sentences and a little courtesy:

> Welcome, Brenda! We’re so glad you’re here and look forward to spending time together.
>

I recommend this version for the bed, plus a direct conversation about the kitchen hours so any early food or medication needs aren’t overlooked.
